Browse trading terms, distinct worksheets and scoped references. Check feature limitations: not every contract or indicator is implemented in the $100,000 virtual simulator.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

A plain-language trading glossary

TradeHQ's glossary explains trading terms in plain English, with worked examples and questions to help you examine the ideas in practice. There are 49 terms in the index, grouped by the part of trading they belong to. The entries discuss limitations as well as the underlying mechanics.

Definitions are written for people who are learning, not for people who already know. Where a term has a contested or marketing-inflated meaning, the entry says so rather than repeating the sales version.

Browse by category
Market Mechanics: Short Squeeze, Liquidation Cascade, Bull Trap, Bear Trap, Whale Manipulation, Stop Loss Hunting, Market Maker, Dark Pool
Technical Analysis: Golden Cross, Death Cross, Fibonacci Retracement, RSI Divergence, MACD Histogram, Bollinger Band Squeeze, Support and Resistance, Candlestick Patterns
Smart Money Concepts: Order Block, Fair Value Gap (FVG)
Chart Patterns: Head and Shoulders, Double Bottom
Trading Fundamentals: Limit Order vs Market Order, Leverage Trading, Margin Call, Liquidation Price, Dollar Cost Averaging, Swing Trading, Day Trading, Scalping
Trading Psychology: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out), FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt), HODL Strategy
Crypto Fundamentals: Satoshi Nakamoto
DeFi: Impermanent Loss, Yield Farming
Why a glossary matters more in trading than in most subjects

Trading vocabulary is unusually hostile to beginners because the same word often carries a precise technical meaning and a loose marketing meaning at the same time. 'Leverage' is a neutral description of borrowed exposure in a textbook and a sales pitch in an advertisement. 'Support' is a level where buyers previously appeared, not a floor that holds. Reading material without pinning down which meaning is in play is how people end up confident about something they have misunderstood.

Each entry here therefore gives a plain definition first, then a longer expert explanation of the mechanics, then the practical caveat that matters when you try to use the idea. Where a concept is popular but weakly evidenced, the entry says so instead of repeating the folklore.

How to use the glossary while practising
Look a term up the first time you meet it rather than guessing from context.
Use a worksheet or an appropriate external dataset for the concept. Check supported chart features first: TradeHQ does not provide every indicator, and generated candles are not historical market evidence.
Use the related-terms links at the bottom of each entry to build a map of the topic.
Practise anything you learn with $100,000 in virtual cash — Educational simulation only — not financial advice.
